annotation.text: So I won't do a lot of reading.
As Trudier said, my book takes up a question of Black poetic form in relation to ideological conflict.
So I'm going to pose a couple of questions.
How is it possible to convince people who see themselves as morally upright, as fundamentally good people,
how do you convince such people to support exploitation, to take part in that?
And particularly when it's not in the long-term interest, even in their own best interest.
My response is misrepresentation, caricature, stereotype.
You convince people that the other, that other group is different,
and therefore not deserving of another form or fair treatment.
That there's separate rules that are permissible when it comes to that group.
And Black poetry has always been caught up in the tension engendered by that.
So, from the first slave poets,
I've got one mind for white folks to see, another for what I know is me.
You don't know. You don't know my mind.
Art for art, figures for figures, all for the white man, none for the nigger.
Many of you have heard them or read them before, so you have them.
But they were so popular on plantations that long after slavery was over with,
people would steal them, steal currant, steal the cider,
enough for people to actually transcribe them.
So at the very onset of our existence here,
poetry's been at the very center of the resistance, ideologically speaking.
So what I want to do is read the preface,
and then what I'll do is go into the discussion.
One night in New Orleans about 20 years ago,
I went to see the Dirty Dozen Brass Band perform at a local bar called the Glass House.
the bar lay in the heart of a working class Black community.
As I recall, the entrance fee was $2, with a two-drink minimum.
Inside, the air was thick with cigarette smoke.
There was little leg space, and the chairs were small and uncomfortable.
There was even a local drunk who had been told the woman sitting next to me was my wife.
But the beauty of the music made me forget these trivialities.
The Dirty Dozen plays what might be called post-modern New Orleans street music.
That is, the music is a unique New Orleans style of jazz.
The band plays classics like Colonial Monk's Blue Monk,
but it superimposes the rhythmic structure of New Orleans marching bands on modern jazz melodies.
The result is a funky music that retains the complexity of jazz compositions
while also compelling one's feet to move.
As if to underscore the primacy of dance,
the band was accompanied by a cadre of dancers who performed along with the music.
I sat there oblivious to the smoke and cramped conditions
enraptured by the performance that featured, at one point,
an eight or nine-year-old Black boy who demonstrated his confidence by playing trumpet with one hand.
After a stellar performance of Miles Davis' All Blues,
one of the dancers noted my enjoyment and said,
Now that's some music. That's some real music.
I ain't never heard that song before in my life, and I'm 23 years old, but that's some music.
In addition to testifying to the creativity of the blues idiom,
the dancer's comments call attention to the importance of style in African American performance.
Though he performed his traditional New Orleans dance known as the Second Line
to the rhythms of a song composed before his birth,
he could appreciate it because it was played in a style that he recognized and understood.
The following study is an attempt to sample and improvise upon the concepts
inscribed within such expressive forms as the Second Line dance,
though many of us have been taught to view such forms as mere entertainment or, worse, as mindless foolishness.
I believe that the Second Line, like the bamboula in the antebellum era,
contains hidden Black codes, indicating cultural resistance in the repressive New World.
At the same time, I do not claim to address all of Black poetry.
Rather, I am interested in analyzing the politics implicit within the historical conditions
that prompt artists to question constructed normality.
Before 1980, for instance, scratching records was considered taboo.
And yet Black and Latino artists transformed this practice into a self-conscious mode of discourse
that challenged the dominant culture's attempt to render them silent and submissive.
Afro-blue is my attempt to situate Black poetry within such practices,
to riff antiphonically on the critical writers who have previously performed similar songs,
and finally to present and represent in the manner of a collage
how the poetic shape by the resistive energy inscribed in scatting and scratching did not just groove.
Rather, the funk expressed in Buddy Bolden's horn, the beautiful pain in Billie Holiday's voice,
and their interrelationships to what I call blues poetics are comprised of histories that are central to my narrative work.
So, the question is, for me, as someone trying to look at this, was,
how do I find out, how do I investigate this question of form?
It was pretty clear that poets who used vernacular form were consistently criticized,
and particularly when you get to the Black Arts Movement,
what you find, for the most part, although there have been some recent efforts,
pretty much either just denunciation on the basis of the fact that writers dared to create new forms.
A classic example is Henry Louis Gates' dismissal of Haki Madhubuti and Amiri Baraka's poetry
on the basis of the fact that much of it was rhetorical.
So, the fact that, and you find this, what I did was I went back,
I wanted to see what the critical attitudes were about the poets.
So, I went all the way back to Brathwaite.
This is 1906 when he's doing this stuff.
But what you find from Brathwaite all the way up to the Black Arts Movement
is a fairly consistent pattern of people criticizing poets on the basis of the form that they use.
So, for instance, Brathwaite, he's a bit uneven.
He's able to accept James Weldon Johnson's God's Trombone and his treatment of the sermon.
He's actually able to, he claims the first book, but he says that God's Trombone,
which contains creation and other forms, was mere transcription.
Then you come to people like Countee Cullen getting to the Harlem Renaissance.
And I'm going to read this one because it's particularly egregious
and I think that you'll see the contradictions therein.
This is his review of Langston Hughes in 1926.
Never having been one to think all subjects in form proper for poetic consideration,
I regard these jazz poems as interlopers in the company of the truly beautiful poems
in other sections of the book.
They move along with the frenzy and electric beat of a Methodist or Baptist revival meeting
and affect me in much the same manner.
The revival meeting excites me, cooling and flushing me with the alternate chills and fevers of emotion.
The cat and the saxophone knock me completely on the side of bewilderment.
In the face of accomplished fact, I cannot say this will never do,
but I feel it ought never to have been done.
People have accused me of beating up on color.
J. Saunders Redding said much the same thing about Hughes' poetry,
particularly the poetry that was based on the blues.
He said that the blues poems were, that they had the expression of the drum,
the iteration actually of the drum, and not the exposition of the piano.
You can see right there the centrality of the drum.
There's a value statement being made.
So form actually has a certain amount of value.
If you look at it within the context of a political economy,
so he says that the blues can only, and the blues and the shout,
There's that dichotomy that's always, always already ascribed to Black folk,
It's as though there is this split between emotions and thought,
and if one is enraptured in emotion, then one is incapable of analyzing.
And we know that nothing could be further from the truth.
There were a whole lot of analysis going on on that drum.
And they banned the drums, and they banned the dances
that corresponded to the music of the drum.
And therein you have sort of the foundation that's set for Black expression,
because subsequently that, if you're a young artist,
you've got to figure out how you're going to respond to that.
You've got to figure out a way.
You don't stop feeling what you feel, and you don't stop thinking what you think.
And remember, if you got caught playing those drums, you'd be put to death.
So you have to figure out a way to get around it.
And most of, I think I read recently that the slaves,
that the median age for slaves in 1850 was something like 17 years old.
So that meant you can get the harsh mentality there.
But also, it's a very thickened generation in terms of age and creativity.
So what you find is, again, you have people like Redding
When you get to the Black Arts Movement,
So what I wanted to do is look at that debate.
And my position, essentially, was that those ideas about art,
about self-determination, about a self-conscious politicized art value,
I took the position that nationalism was a bit narrow in the way
that they looked at the kinds of problems.
So what I wanted to do is try to talk about these ideas.
And what I found was that in many ways, the writers of the 60s
in some ways I think they even, that they even theorized.
Because what they wanted, what they were talking about,
was a national poetry, an African American national poetics.
And they sensed that there was something valuable in vernacular culture.
So for me, what I realized, having read a very important essay,
my book in some ways is a kind of a riff on Sherley Anne Williams' essay,
The Blues Roots of Contemporary Afro-American Poetry.
And what she said was that you could look at the musicians as a metaphor,
that the musicians extend musical traditions in much the same way
as the poets extend verbal traditions or verbal forms.
So for me, that became, and she's clearly elaborating
Stephen Henderson's ideas and understanding of New Black poetry,
where he talks about mass comm and the poem as a score,
something that, where poets wouldn't necessarily use the print form of a poem
as his only guide or her only guide,
because it could vary in the vibes, etc.
So for me, what I did was come up with a blues model.
My essential argument is that if you really want to understand
the ways that many African American poets approach form
and the creative process, that we can look to the three bodies of blues
In the early portion, the first attempts you find with Paul Laurence Dunbar
and later Langston Hughes, Sterling Brown,
where they're taking specific stanza forms,
or you find people taking Black speech patterns
and not simply transcribing them onto the page,
but attempting to represent the speech patterns of the folk
in such a way that unifies and captures the rhythmic patterns and cadences,
the imagery of what they have to say.
Zora Neale Hurston did something similar in 1937,
in Their Eyes Were Watching God.
So you have people like Sterling Brown,
for those of you who don't know that famous poem,
Steady bow, ain't no rush baby, long ways to go.
So you get that kind of, and clearly there's no stereotyping.
Before this time, you really don't have,
there's a kind of confusion between Black vernacular speech patterns on one hand
People felt that if a poet wrote in the vernacular,
that it was simply because of that stereotype.
And they weren't able to differentiate between literary discourse
or vernacular as a component of that,
They were really afraid, I think, of that.
And what's at stake here, what's the problem that I see,
is a version of class politics where, particularly you saw it in color,
where there's this sense that if it isn't legitimate,
if it isn't expressed by the dominant culture,
or what we call the ideological state apparatus,
if it isn't circulated through that,
and of course, people don't go around thinking this,
but these are the kinds of ideas that people are operating on.
So jazz isn't capable, again, of thought,
So after Colin responds to Hughes,
you have Hughes writing his essay,
Negro Artist on a Racial Mountain,
the poets go on, an experiment.
Hughes himself comes up in 1951 with Montage of a Dream Deferred,
and here you have a different type of poetry.
where you have poets fusing their concerns for the vernacular
with conventional notions of literature, imagery.
You have snatches of titles, allusions,
Stephen Henderson used the term mascom,
and his idea was that there were certain words in Black culture
that carried a great deal of weight.
So you'd find repetitions throughout the culture,
and then you've got Snoop Dogg,
So the term roll, certain titles that tend to affect us,
and what I think he was talking about
is that music and the language is a repository of cultural memory.
So a snatch of one poem where you might think about the title here,
It Don't Mean a Thing if It Ain't Got That Swing,
On the Good Foot, Like Jitterbugs,
Got to be Jelly, Cause Jam,
So you have, and I think most poets
combine various aspects of the vernacular
and so depending on the individual,
this can manifest itself in a lot of different ways.
most people seemed to believe that there wasn't any form
Now, I had actually been in a Black writer's workshop
I was the youngest member of the workshop,
and they made sure that I remembered that.
And one of the people in that workshop
So I heard people talk about their poems,
their ideas, at a fairly early stage.
So I always knew that there was a form and a technique.
The question had to do with how do I come to grips with this,
and how do I translate that for readers,
because the jazz musician was an important model,
So how do you write about that in a way that makes sense?
I began to read performance theory,
and just thinking about the music itself,
I found a concept of what we call paralinguistics.
calls the African American version of that,
But what paralinguistics are referred to
in which the sound goes on to mean
Singing is a form of paralinguistics.
this is endemic to Black vernacular thought.
Long before African Americans came here,
where the instrumentalists mimic the human voice,
and singers and poets have recreated,
And so what we find in hip-hop today
is simply the most recent form of that.
I came up with the idea
that writers who use this form of poetry
or they try to incarnate secular priesthood.
And say, well, what's that got to do with me?
if you look at the musicians,
and the way that the musicians are respected
the way audiences think about them,
I've just been told I'm out of time.
But what I will say in concluding this
is that that form of poetics
and I think the ideas are very much alive and well.
: We'd like to thank our panelists for their presentations.
I think everybody can hear me.
And what we'd like to do now,
I want to pose a couple questions to the panelists
and then we'll open this up to the entire audience.
You heard Maryemma say that Dunbar mastered the art
and you heard Hilary raise the question
and then suggesting that Lucille Clifton wrote for the poem
instead of thinking about those audiences.
I want to turn the question back to think about the poet a bit more
and ask our panelists to think,
What are the stresses on poetic creativity
that are imposed from the outside,
that are imposed from the inside?
If you're a poet writing in 2004,
and you might be Lucille Clifton writing for the poem,
but there are other issues as well.
If we could sort of capsulize a few of those issues
at the beginning of the conversation here.
: I'll take a stab at it.
I'm currently teaching a course using,
as a bunch of material, of course, on slavery.
And one of the things that I'm struck by is the idea,
and I guess James Olden has written about it,
this triangular relationship that affected the narrative.
That is, the audience, the sponsor,
and the publication of the text itself.
And I think that we can actually think about that relationship
with contemporary publishing, the contemporary text.
That is, the audience, the sponsor,
and the text itself are in this triangular relationship.
And the balance, I think, varies.
That is, some people write more toward the audience.
Some people are more in touch with what the kind of sponsorship
or publication venue, the expectations of that.
And then other people, or the same people at different times,
really want to push a particular form or theme in the text.
So I think that the answer is more complex in terms of the shift
that has occurred, that the balance between those three things
varies from poem to poem, or poet to poet.
And depending on what part of your career you might have to be in.
I don't like to use the word purists,
but I think that people make those kinds of choices.
That if I'm not going to write for the marketplace,
it might take me longer, and I'm going to do it this way.
I think that people make those choices pretty much based on
Sometimes a career at the beginning, and you hear people make
I used to think, but now I do.
So I think that that kind of thing makes it a little bit more complicated
for us to set a particular paradigm on how it's done.
But I do think those three factors are still very much concerns.
: Well, I think that makes a lot of sense.
And I do think that writing the poem, serving the poem,
is a lot easier said than done.
And I think Clifton would certainly acknowledge that, too.
One way to approach all of this is to be a poet of pluralistic influences.
I don't think that any poet, no matter what his or her race or ethnicity
or sexual orientation or gender might be,
should think that their influences will come just from one particular camp.
You can't escape all the influences coming at you from every different direction.
Lucille Clifton has said that when she was growing up,
the writers who were especially important to her were Thomas Wolfe
Those are surprising writers, I think, for her to cite time and again
as having been important to her.
Sometimes you can't always choose your influences.
It's a matter of what you do with those influences.
Once you reach a certain age, of course, you can choose influences.
You can choose African-American precursors and models.
And whether you're Black or white or some other race or ethnicity,
see what you can do with those.
But I think it's a matter of staying flexible and acknowledging,
as Maryemma said, that people do change.
That's our right as human beings.
That comes with the territory of being human.
And so enjoy the changes that you go through as a poet.
And although the marketplace may not like who you become, so what?
They may come along later and look back at those changes
as being the seminal moment in your career.
I think about Adrienne Rich and her development as a poet
and how mistrustful critics were when she published
What's she doing there with her poetry?
But in later years, people look back at that volume
as her greatest work to that point.
So sometimes the role of a poet involves educating the audiences
instead of playing to the market.
See if you can raise your audience to your level,
: Well, I think that what you said about transformation
and how ultimately what you do with the idea is a good one.
I suppose, for me, I'm rather suspicious of the marketplace
as a kind of barometer for what people or how successful people are.
And sometimes, you know, I had a great friend named Tom Denton.
Tom used to tell me that your assets and your liabilities
So sometimes you don't want certain people to like what you're doing.
It might not be a good idea.
That's the way I see it.
I think when we talk about art,
But at the same time, people have to do what they feel they need to do.
I do think that it's important for people not to be naive,
or at least be able to deal with consequences.
I mean, we don't live in a meaning-free society.
So people are going to respond one way or another.
I don't think there's any neutral position on that either.
You dealt with all of those issues, the three things there.
Hilary says that the poet can bring the audience along.
And Tony says that you should be who you are, write what you want.
But let's consider the reality in 2004.
Lots of young people, those poets under 30,
whom Hilary had to raise their hands.
They don't have the option of bringing people along.
And when you think about commercialization,
and you think about technological influences on what they're doing,
pressures on them to get things out if they want to be published.
How do you average technology commercialization,
somebody mentioned that earlier, into this whole picture?
Well, you know, I was glad you asked that.
Because I do think that the direction of poetry is changing in some parts.
We have the net now in terms of publishing,
even more than publishing, certainly changing.
But on some level, this is not new.
She used to be an editor, as you know.
So most Black writers until very, very recently
always had to have a job.
I remember people saying, well, they called it a trade.
And then your real work was your writing.
William Carlos Williams was a doctor.
So, I mean, the idea that your work has to sell,
I mean, now, this is imperialism.
So the question of – I think for me, I'm more concerned with how is it
that people are able to be productive?
And what is it going to take?
And that's probably an individual kind of thing.
What is it going to take for people to continue to produce?
And if you can find somebody to pay you for what you do,
But, again, it's very difficult to get somebody to pay you loads of money anyway
for ultimately a representation that challenges the way that you've been taught
In other words, how you get your master – it's hard to pay your master –
get your master to pay you for telling him, look, I don't want to be a slave anymore.
But it also appears to me that we have such a broad range of venues today,
both high technology, whether it's the internet, the web,
but also we have the sound.
One of the things that I was interested in is what happened around the 1940s and 50s.
I think you talked a little bit about this too.
When radio began to put what was in private homes,
what we used to call records, remember those?
You can hear it on the radio.
So what would happen if, which is actually what's happening now,
if poetry had that same venue that early?
Now it's got it now because, as I said, I came in last night
and I should have been asleep, but I'm watching that poetry jam
because I like to watch it and it's interesting to me.
But I'm hearing it, and I think the sound aspect of it is what is –
and I don't want to use the word performance because that gets into a whole other thing,
but just the very fact that people hear it has changed it more than anything else.
I think that leads to more performance.
That leads, but it's if you can imagine using radio,
because that's an earlier form of technology,
and what it did to music, what it did for music, what it did with music,
or go back even further in the 1920s when people were doing with race records.
So each of those moments there's been change in the form
because of change in the distribution, and so those things are affected.
So I think we might, I think Herman Weaver's talked a little bit about this notion of sound
as opposed to the spoken word.
When we talk about oral, we also hear aural, and to distinguish between those two things.
So I think that we're getting into, obviously, questions of poetics,
and they're very difficult and complex issues.
And so we tend to talk about the oral tradition a little bit.
Well, the oral tradition has its own sort of mix of things.
So what you heard me say was, I'm getting old, y'all got to do more work.
On some of these questions, because I'm not going to live long enough to finish the work.
I'm glad you folks are here, but we need to bring some more people on board to do this kind of work.
And this requires studying in a wide range of fields, whether it's linguistics or what have you.
We need a lot more work to examine those cultural aspects.
So some of that is what I've been thinking about.
: Well, I would just add to that that I think it's very different.
Do you want to try to be a famous poet, or do you want to try to be a great poet?
They're not necessarily one and the same.
And I think that Tony gets at that by bringing up Walt Whitman.
And it will only be a very lucky few in any generation to be called both great and famous.
I wonder how many here in this audience today are great poets, but they never achieve Gordon Anthology fame.
It's our loss if that's the case.
But we live in a time when the literary marketplace is so fragmented that it's really going to be tough to join the ranks of Toni Morrison.
Maybe prose is the way to go.
But maybe if what you're really looking for is enduring fame, maybe try the novel.
Let novel writing be your trade.
It wouldn't be the first time for a writer to try that.
And I know this sounds sentimental.
But I do think it's important to aim to be a good poet before you aim to be a well-known poet.
